# Pack 3 — Full

This file contains the complete selected rule blocks. No additional reference reads are required.

## 1. Begin sentences with subjects and verbs.

Requirement: Begin each declarative sentence with its main-clause subject and finite verb. Move background clauses and introductory detours into the middle. Keep the subject and verb together. Questions retain interrogative syntax; commands begin with the imperative verb.

Pass: The reader reaches the subject and main action before any background detour.

## 2. Order words for emphasis.

Requirement: Use 2–3–1 in every sentence under editorial control. Rank the emphatic words or phrases: 1 = most important; 2 = second most important; 3 = everything else. Put 2 at the beginning, 3 in the middle, and 1 at the end. End on the strongest word or phrase. Move trailing context and qualifications into the middle or a preceding sentence without changing their scope. Rewrite the syntax until this order holds.

Pass: Label the opening 2 and the ending 1; all remaining information sits between them. Nothing trails the strongest ending except punctuation.

Example: “Checkout latency fell by 40% in the staging test” buries the result. Write: “Checkout latency fell in the staging test by 40%.” The opening names the second-ranked idea; the ending carries the first-ranked result; the test context stays in the middle.

## 3. Activate your verbs.

Requirement: Put the action in a specific verb. Replace action nominalizations and their carrier verbs: “conducted a review” becomes “reviewed”; “made a decision” becomes “decided.” Use the actor as the subject except in the defined passive-voice cases in Rule 4.

Pass: Every action has a direct verb; every remaining passive construction passes Rule 4.

## 4. Be passive-aggressive.

Requirement: Use passive voice only when the actor is unknown, the actor is irrelevant to the reported result, or the affected person or thing is the established topic. In every other case, use active voice and identify the actor. Preserve responsibility when the evidence identifies a responsible party.

Pass: Every passive construction has one of the three stated reasons; none conceals known, relevant responsibility.

## 5. Watch those adverbs.

Requirement: Delete adverbs that merely intensify or repeat the verb's meaning. Replace a weak verb plus a manner adverb with the precise verb. Retain an adverb only when it changes the factual meaning, scope, frequency, degree, or timing; preserve qualifiers such as “approximately” and “partly.”

Pass: Each surviving adverb contributes information lost on deletion; no verb–adverb pair substitutes for an available precise verb.

## 6. Take it easy on the -ings.

Requirement: Express completed actions with finite verbs. Retain a progressive construction only for action genuinely in progress, and retain a participial construction only when its subject and timing are explicit. Replace chains of -ing actions with finite clauses in the actual sequence.

Pass: Every progressive encodes ongoing action; every participle has the correct subject; no -ing chain conceals chronology.

## 7. Fear not the long sentence.

Requirement: Give every long sentence one main-clause spine; attach its details in a traceable order. Keep connected material in that sentence rather than splitting it solely because of word count. Split at a change of actor, time, or logic that otherwise obscures the relationship.

Pass: The main clause and each attachment are identifiable on one reading; sentence length alone has not determined a cut.

## 8. Establish a pattern, then give it a twist.

Requirement: Use parallel grammatical forms for equivalent items. In a setup-and-turn sequence, establish the repeated form before the turn, then place the pattern-breaking item last. Make that item carry the change in meaning.

Pass: Equivalent items are parallel; a deliberate break occurs at the turn rather than by accident.

## 9. Let punctuation control pace and space.

Requirement: Use a period to close a thought, a colon after a complete clause to introduce its explanation or expansion, a semicolon to join independent clauses, and paired punctuation to enclose an interruption. Use commas to mark grammatical boundaries. Match each mark to the relationship it expresses.

Pass: Each punctuation mark has a grammatical job; no comma splice, unclosed pair, or ornamental interruption remains.

## 10. Cut big, then small.

Requirement: Cut in this order: off-purpose sections, duplicated paragraphs, redundant sentences, expendable phrases, then expendable words. Preserve unique evidence, qualifications, required details, and steps the reader needs. Complete the structural cuts before line polishing.

Pass: Every remaining passage contributes a distinct claim, evidence, transition, characterization, or required action.

## 11. Prefer the simple over the technical.

Requirement: Use the simplest word that preserves the exact meaning. Replace jargon with its plain equivalent. Retain a specialist term when it names a distinction the plain replacement loses; define it on first use for a nonexpert audience. Keep code identifiers exact.

Pass: Each specialist term is necessary for precision or is an exact identifier; unfamiliar necessary terms are defined for the reader.

## 12. Give key words their space.

Requirement: Use a distinctive emphatic word once in its local passage; reserve its next occurrence for deliberate recurrence under Rule 33. Remove accidental nearby echoes. Use the same technical name for the same thing throughout; do not create false distinctions through synonym swapping.

Pass: Repeated emphatic words have an identifiable structural role; repeated entity names remain consistent.

## 13. Play with words, even in serious stories.

Requirement: In playful prose, build wordplay from the subject's actual vocabulary and make its literal meaning intelligible. In serious prose, create verbal play through parallelism, sound, or a precise contrast rather than a joke at the subject's expense. Keep condolence, emergency, and strictly factual status text literal.

Pass: Expressive prose has a subject-based verbal pattern or turn; protected literal forms contain no inserted joke.

## 14. Get the name of the dog.

Requirement: Replace a generic description of a central person, place, object, or event with a concrete identifying detail from the source. Use the actual name, number, model, action, or observable feature. Record a missing detail as an evidence gap rather than filling it with invention.

Pass: Central descriptions contain sourced specifics; every added nonfiction detail is supported or explicitly marked as missing.

## 15. Pay attention to names.

Requirement: Check every name, title, label, and spelling against the source. Introduce people and components unambiguously, then name them consistently. Apply requested anonymization consistently. Give fictional characters distinct names and keep the name-to-character mapping stable.

Pass: Each name identifies one referent, matches its source or fictional assignment, and follows the chosen naming convention.

## 16. Seek original images.

Requirement: Replace a stock metaphor with a concrete observation or a new comparison derived from the subject. For each comparison, identify the exact shared property. Keep one coherent image instead of mixing incompatible comparisons.

Pass: Every image supplies a specific correspondence; no stock or mixed metaphor survives.

## 17. Riff on the creative language of others.

Requirement: When borrowing language, distinguish quotation, paraphrase, and allusion. Quote exactly and credit the source; restate paraphrases in original wording and attribute distinctive borrowed ideas. Build the new passage around the present subject rather than copying another writer's expression.

Pass: Borrowed language has a clear source and form; new language does new work rather than masquerading as an original quotation.

## 18. Set the pace with sentence length.

Requirement: Mark changes of direction with short independent sentences. Carry a continuous sequence in connected clauses. Change sentence length at an argumentative or narrative turn instead of repeating one sentence shape throughout.

Pass: The cadence changes at each turn; continuous action and decisive stops have different sentence shapes.

## 19. Vary the lengths of paragraphs.

Requirement: Give each paragraph one topic or narrative beat. Start a new paragraph when that job changes. Put a pivotal takeaway in a one-sentence paragraph and develop its evidence in surrounding paragraphs. In a one-paragraph format, preserve the format and mark the turn within it.

Pass: Paragraph breaks follow changes of job; the pivotal point is visibly distinguished without violating the requested format.

## 20. Choose the number of elements with a purpose in mind.

Requirement: Build series by function: one for focus, two for contrast, three for a completed pattern, four or more for inventory or accumulation. Give every item a distinct role. Retain every item the user requires; remove filler added only to reach a count.

Pass: The series count corresponds to its function; no duplicate or invented item exists solely to make a pattern.

## 21. Know when to back off and when to show off.

Requirement: Describe harm, grief, danger, and major factual results with concrete nouns and direct verbs. Remove evaluative intensifiers and decorative commentary from those passages. In explanatory or playful passages, make each flourish carry a comparison, distinction, or insight.

Pass: High-stakes passages let the facts carry the weight; every flourish elsewhere adds identifiable meaning.

## 22. Climb up and down the ladder of abstraction.

Requirement: Pair each central abstract claim with a concrete example, observation, or measurement. Explain what the example establishes and where that inference stops. Connect concrete detail back to the general point instead of leaving either level unsupported.

Pass: The reader can move from claim to example and back; the inference does not exceed the evidence.

## 23. Tune your voice.

Requirement: Set person, register, attitude, and distance from the brief or supplied draft. Keep them consistent throughout. Preserve the author's deliberate conversational expressions while correcting the prose around them. Read the finished text for shifts into an unrequested register.

Pass: The voice matches the brief from opening to ending; edits have not replaced the author's voice with generic formal prose.

## 24. Work from a plan.

Requirement: Before drafting, write a working outline that states the opening, the job of each section, and the ending. For a short message, use one line. For revision, map the existing structure before moving material. Make the final sequence match the plan or update the plan to match the corrected sequence.

Pass: Every section has a defined job and position; the whole has an opening-to-ending route.

## 25. Learn the difference between reports and stories.

Requirement: Classify the piece before drafting. Report: give the answer or current status first, then evidence and action. Story: show a disruption, consequential action, and change. Hybrid: give the report's answer first, then a clearly bounded narrative. Apply narrative rules within story passages only.

Pass: The opening and sequence follow the declared form; operational answers are not withheld to manufacture suspense.

## 26. Use dialogue as a form of action.

Requirement: Make every exchange change a decision, relationship, obstacle, or the reader's knowledge. Cut dialogue that repeats narration without advancing the scene. In nonfiction, use documented wording inside quotation marks and summarize undocumented exchanges without quotation marks.

Pass: Every exchange changes something; every nonfiction quotation is traceable to its source.

## 27. Reveal traits of character.

Requirement: Establish a character trait through an observable choice, action, habit, or sacrifice before naming the trait. Keep judgments about motive separate from reported behavior. Use more than a trait label to distinguish the person.

Pass: Each stated trait has behavioral evidence; inferred motives are identified as inferences rather than reported facts.

## 28. Put odd and interesting things next to each other.

Requirement: Place the two sides of a contrast in adjacent sentences or paragraphs. Identify the shared comparison axis and state the revealing difference. Preserve mismatched baselines and uncertainty explicitly instead of implying equivalence.

Pass: The contrasting facts are adjacent, comparable on a named basis, and not presented as an unsupported causal relationship.

## 29. Foreshadow dramatic events and powerful conclusions.

Requirement: In a story, introduce the detail or question that prepares the major turn before the turn occurs. Bring it back at the payoff. Distinguish evidence available at the time from hindsight; use only sourced clues in nonfiction.

Pass: Each major narrative payoff has an earlier setup; setup and payoff match the actual record.

## 30. To generate suspense, use internal cliffhangers.

Requirement: At an internal story-section break, end on an unresolved consequence, obstacle, or question. Resolve it in the subsequent narrative. Keep the promised stakes equal to the actual payoff. In reports and instructions, give the needed answer immediately instead.

Pass: Every internal narrative cliffhanger has a later payoff; no operational answer is delayed for suspense.

## 31. Build your work around a key question.

Requirement: Write the central question in a working note before drafting. Make each section answer it, supply necessary evidence, or resolve a supporting question. Remove material with none of those jobs. For a reference document, use the reader's common lookup need as the question.

Pass: Every section has a direct relationship to the central question; the ending answers it or states the evidence gap.

## 32. Place gold coins along the path.

Requirement: Give every substantive section a concrete reader payoff: a revealing fact, useful example, resolved question, actionable instruction, or new implication. Distribute those payoffs through the piece instead of saving all value for the ending.

Pass: Every substantive section delivers identifiable new value; none consists solely of setup or repetition.

## 33. Repeat, repeat, and repeat.

Requirement: Repeat the central term at the opening, a major transition, and the conclusion of a multi-section piece. Give the recurrence a new job each time: establish, develop, resolve. In shorter pieces, repeat only for reference or an explicit rhetorical pattern. Keep wording stable for the same concept.

Pass: Long-form recurrence follows establish–develop–resolve; every other repetition has a reference or pattern function.

## 34. Write from different cinematic angles.

Requirement: In scene-based writing, move through three scales: orient the setting, show the participant's action, then isolate a telling detail. Signal changes of place or viewpoint. Build every nonfiction scale from documented observation.

Pass: Scenes contain setting, action, and detail; the reader can identify the viewpoint and any change of scale.

## 35. Report and write for scenes.

Requirement: Build each scene from time, place, participants, action, and a resulting change. Use scenes for pivotal events and summary for intervening time. If the nonfiction source lacks scene-level evidence, retain factual summary and record the missing evidence.

Pass: Every scene has all five elements and sourced nonfiction details; missing observations remain gaps, not inventions.

## 36. Mix narrative modes.

Requirement: Use scene for a pivotal event, summary to cross uneventful time, and exposition to supply a necessary explanation. Put exposition at the point its information is needed. Mark each change of time, place, or mode.

Pass: Each passage's mode matches its job; transitions preserve chronology and orientation.

## 37. In short works, don't waste a syllable.

Requirement: For a short-form brief, remove preambles, repeated context, redundant modifiers, and closing restatements. Give each word an informational, grammatical, rhythmic, or voice-preserving job. Meet the requested length without sacrificing necessary qualifications or unique facts.

Pass: The text meets its length limit, preserves the required meaning, and contains no removable setup or repetition.

## 38. Prefer archetypes to stereotypes.

Requirement: Ground a recognizable role in the individual's actions, circumstances, and contradictions. Replace stock trait bundles with the person's specific behavior. Use demographic facts only as facts; establish personality and motive from separate evidence.

Pass: The individual is distinguishable from the role; no trait or motive rests solely on demographic membership.

## 39. Write toward an ending.

Requirement: Choose the final answer, decision, action, resolution, or image before polishing. Make the preceding material prepare it. End immediately after delivering it. Place essential qualifications before the final emphasis and preserve their scope.

Pass: The ending completes the opening promise, introduces no unsupported claim, and has no trailing generic recap.

## 40. Draft a mission statement for your work.

Requirement: Before drafting or revising, write one working sentence: “For [reader], this piece will [purpose] so they can [result].” Use it to decide what belongs. Keep the mission out of the deliverable unless requested.

Pass: The working mission identifies reader, purpose, and result; the finished piece fulfills that same mission.

## 41. Turn procrastination into rehearsal.

Requirement: When blocked, rehearse one opening or speak through one version of the argument in a working note. Then write a provisional draft from it. Move unresolved details into marked gaps instead of restarting preparation.

Pass: A blocked start produces draft text after rehearsal rather than another planning loop.

## 42. Do your homework well in advance.

Requirement: Before writing new factual material, identify and obtain the evidence for its key claims. Record source locations and unresolved gaps. For a supplied-text rewrite, use the supplied facts; verify any added claim before including it. Finish evidence collection before polishing factual claims.

Pass: Every added factual claim has a source; every unresolved dependency is marked rather than fabricated.

## 43. Read for both form and content.

Requirement: When using a model text, extract its argument and separately map its opening, evidence order, transitions, cadence, and ending. Reuse the structural technique in new wording. Keep claims from the model separate from verified facts for the current piece.

Pass: Content and form have separate working notes; borrowed structure does not become copied prose or unsourced evidence.

## 44. Save string.

Requirement: Capture reusable facts, observations, phrases, and questions in an authorized working note with provenance and date. Separate verified material from leads. Persist reusable context in the approved destination; retain task-only scraps in working notes.

Pass: Saved material has provenance, a date, and a fact-versus-lead label; nothing is persisted to an unauthorized destination.

## 45. Break long projects into parts.

Requirement: Divide a multi-section project into units with a defined job, inputs, and completion condition. Draft each against the shared brief and terminology. Reassemble the units and remove duplicate claims, missing links, and inconsistent terminology.

Pass: Every unit has a completion condition; the assembled piece is connected and internally consistent.

## 46. Take an interest in all crafts that support your work.

Requirement: Identify the supporting work required by the deliverable: reporting, calculation, fact-checking, visualization, layout, or editing. Complete and verify each dependency before claiming the piece is finished. Explicitly identify any dependency that the available evidence or tools cannot satisfy.

Pass: Each required supporting task is completed with evidence or disclosed as unresolved; none is silently assumed done.

## 47. Recruit your own support group.

Requirement: Run a reader check before delivery: ask whether the intended reader can state the point, follow the sequence, and identify the ending or action. Use an authorized independent reviewer when one is available; otherwise perform and label a self-review. Never report self-review as independent feedback.

Pass: The three reader questions are answered; feedback provenance identifies an actual reviewer or self-review.

## 48. Limit self-criticism in early drafts.

Requirement: Complete a beginning-to-ending draft before line editing. Mark uncertainty in working notes and continue. After the complete draft exists, run the structural and sentence-level passes. Keep generating and judging as separate phases.

Pass: A complete draft precedes polishing; all temporary factual gaps are resolved or disclosed before delivery.

## 49. Learn from your critics.

Requirement: For each critique received, identify the specific reader problem and the passage causing it. Correct factual errors. Apply editorial changes that fix the identified problem while preserving the brief. Account for a rejected recommendation with a concrete conflict or evidence-based reason.

Pass: Every criticism is addressed by a correction or a stated reason; none is ignored or accepted without examining the passage.

## 50. Own the tools of your craft.

Requirement: Treat every rule in the active pack as the writing standard. Identify violations by rule number, repair them, and recheck the result. Keep authored rule wording in the numbered reference files; regenerate pack excerpts after edits. Select the pack through the skill's routing procedure, never by dropping a rule that is difficult to satisfy.

Pass: The final audit accounts for the active pack: all 55 rules in Full. Every departure within that scope cites an explicit user override rather than editorial preference.

## 51. Take advantage of narrative numbers.

Requirement: Attach units and timeframes to quantities. Give changes their baseline and comparison period. Distinguish counts, rates, percent changes, and percentage-point changes. Label estimates, extrapolations, and realized results. Verify each derived calculation and pair consequential figures with a concrete comparison from the evidence.

Pass: Every number has interpretable scope; comparisons and arithmetic are correct; projections remain labeled as projections.

## 52. Express your best thought in the shortest sentence.

Requirement: State the central insight in a standalone sentence. Make it the shortest complete authored sentence in the piece; exact source quotations are outside that comparison. Move supporting explanation around it while preserving any qualification that determines its truth. Apply Rule 2 to its word order.

Pass: The central insight occupies the shortest complete authored sentence and remains accurate on its own.

## 53. Match your diction to your writing purpose.

Requirement: Set the register from the brief, then use words from that register throughout. Use conversational words for conversation, precise domain terms for experts, and formal wording for formal deliverables. Translate imported jargon and remove corporate filler unless it is an exact name or required quotation.

Pass: Vocabulary matches the purpose and audience; every register change follows an explicit change in speaker or form.

## 54. Create a mosaic of detail to reveal character.

Requirement: For a character portrait, combine details from different categories: action, speech, habit, possessions, relationships, or a contradiction. Make each detail add a different facet. Replace multiple examples of the same trait with complementary evidence.

Pass: The portrait contains more than one facet; every nonfiction detail is sourced and no inferred motive is presented as observation.

## 55. Look for the “inciting incident” to kick-start your story.

Requirement: Start a story with the event that disrupts the prior situation and triggers the central action. Put necessary backstory after that event. In a hybrid, place the story's trigger immediately after the report lead. Preserve the actual event, stakes, and sequence in nonfiction.

Pass: The narrative opens on a specific disruption with a consequence; backstory does not delay the trigger.
